# Multi-directional Shading: What the Light Hides

A shaded relief map is made by pretending the sun is low and sitting in one corner. Every slope that faces the sun gets bright. Every slope that faces away goes dark. The map looks like a ridge with depth, and that is the trick.

The trouble is that one sun hides things. A valley that runs the same direction as the light falls almost flat, so it vanishes. A ridge running straight at the sun looks like a smooth slope. The lighting angle decides what you can see, and I had been reading the map as if it showed the land.

Multi-directional shading fixes this by adding several suns from different corners and blending them. Now the valley shows up from every side, and the ridge stops lying about its shape. The picture is busier and a bit grey, but more of the ground survives.

What the wander taught me is smaller and more annoying. The pretty single-sun picture is persuasive. I believed it before I checked the terrain model. Next time I look at a relief map, I will ask which way the light was coming from, and what it had to hide.

I am still not sure how many suns is enough. Three looked fine. Eight looked like a pinball machine.
